extracted.intended_audience: poets, literary critics, and students of poetry and poetics
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for judging or composing high-quality poetry: intellectual depth, relation of thought to imagination, diction, metre, imagery, polish, and the proper study of models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth and energy of thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Depth, and energy of thought: 'No man was ever yet a great poet, without being at the same time a profound philosopher.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry should show profound intellectual energy — thought that wrestles with knowledge, passions, and emotions. Anti-patterns: merely meteoric flashes of imaginative power without sustained intellectual depth, which yield transitory brilliance rather than greatness. Examples in text: distinction between shallow works (e.g., some early poems) and Shakespeare/Milton, where thought is profound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fusion of creative power and intellectual energy
rubrics_metrics.description: The creative power and the intellectual energy should be reconciled and work together rather than one extinguishing the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Great poets balance imaginative force with reflective thought; each may threaten the other in excess but in masterpieces they blend—'like two rapid streams...blend, and dilate, and flow on in one current and with one voice.' Anti-pattern: works where imagination overwhelms thought (giving spectacle without meaning) or vice versa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mastery/dominium over language
rubrics_metrics.description: Perfect dominion of language — the poet's language must be mastered so that knowledge becomes habitual and intuitive and language wedded to feeling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Language should be under the poet's full control, enabling expressive range and unity of voice. Guidance includes patient study and minute understanding; anti-pattern: being 'no mere child of nature' — a passive vehicle of inspiration without craft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate integration of philosophical matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophy in poetry must be harmonized with poetry — 'fused into the poetic mass' and introduced so it appeals to the heart and moral being.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflective or philosophical elements should be integrated obliquely or tenderly, in service of human action and passion. Anti-pattern: overexplicit speculative science or archaic lore that dates the poem (Dante's dead thirteenth-century lore is given as an instance of science that should be avoided when it becomes obsolete). Example: Milton's handling of philosophy is praised as harmonized with poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of ephemeral or technical scientific detail
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet should avoid science which is 'ever in a process of change and development, and abide by the fixed and eternal.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not weigh poems down with contemporary scientific or technical details that will become obsolete; favor eternal, human truths and reflections. Anti-pattern: embedding then-current scientific lore that makes the poem unintelligible or dated in later ages (as criticised in Dante's Paradiso passages).

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity combined with exquisite polish
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim for 'exquisite polish of the diction, combined with perfect simplicity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use refined, carefully positioned words while maintaining naturalness and simplicity; avoid words that a gentleman would not use in dignified conversation or phrases only a learned man would use. The polished style should not betray artifice. Anti-pattern: meretricious finery or affected diction that tricks rather than communicates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purity and jealous care for the native tongue
rubrics_metrics.description: Guard the purity of the native tongue: language is 'the armory of the human mind'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Protect idiomatic and native usages; be precise and avoid improprieties of word usage that cloud meaning. The text invokes Dante's De la volgare eloquenza and Hobbesian warnings against impropriety of words. Anti-pattern: corrupting or needlessly exoticizing diction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Melodic harmony and metrical intelligence
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction and metre should be constructed with meditation and intelligent purpose rather than mechanical convenience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measures and metrical movement should show countless modifications and subtle balances of sound, contributing to melody and emphasis. Avoid adopting mechanical or overpowering foreign metres that impose a tune distracting from meaning (example: borrowed Germanic metres likened to 'galloping over a paved road').

rubrics_metrics.name: Variety produced by subtle modification, not crude novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Variety in metres and sounds should come from countless modifications and subtle balances rather than from introducing wholly new, overpowering metres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The older bards achieved charming variety through refined adjustments in common national metres. Anti-pattern: adopting meters that have a specific overpowering tune which invites attention to rhythm at the expense of sense (example stanza given as an overpowering metre).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of imagery: general polish vs specificity
rubrics_metrics.description: Older poets often used general imagery (sun, moon, flowers, streams) and derived excellence from 'the manner of treating them' rather than novelty of subject; modern poets tend toward specific portraiture and striking images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choosing between general, universal images and specific, novel images depends on aim; excellence can arise from superior treatment of familiar motifs. Anti-pattern: exotic specificity with careless diction or metre that undermines poetic quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete adequateness of manner to matter (unity/entireness)
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'satisfying entireness' — a complete adequateness of the manner to the matter — is an important poetic quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Form, diction, metre, and imagery should fit the subject so the poem feels whole and adequate. Examples: comparisons to Anacreon and Catullus where manner perfectly suits small materials; anti-pattern: mismatch between style and substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of foreground, middle, and background (compositional focus)
rubrics_metrics.description: In composition, the foreground and middle objects should be determinate and engaging rather than throwing main interest into inaccessible background.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure poems so the primary interest is accessible and developed; avoid compositions where attention is trapped looking backward or where the 'main interest' is obscured in the far background (landscape-painting analogy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grace — pervasive, perfusive, omnipresent
rubrics_metrics.description: Perfusive and omnipresent 'grace' is a preserved and precious quality in earlier masters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate an effortless-seeming grace that pervades diction, imagery, and movement. This quality contributes to lasting charm (examples: Anacreon, Catullus). Anti-pattern: works lacking pervasive grace even if they show technical skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Study of the best models and cultivation of taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Good taste and excellence are the result of thought and 'the submissive study of the best models'; reputation matured by ages is a guide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Learn by close study of canonical masters (classical and established models). Appeal to the accumulated judgment of ages: the works that stand the test of time offer instruction. Examples: references to Reynolds and Harris on acquiring just taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of meretricious ornament and triviality
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject 'soiled and over-worn finery of the meretricious muse' and trivial thought dressed in enigmatic expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid superficial ornament that masks meagre thought; prefer clarity and genuine expression over fashionable affectation. Anti-pattern: prose and verse that strive to be 'poetical' solely via perfunctory ornament or obscure phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional authenticity and moral appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry should appeal to the heart and moral being — convey pity, pathos, moral and spiritual maxims — without merely fabricating visions of wrath or bitterness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emotional material must be authentic and connected to human sympathies; beware of excessive bitterness or presumption in moral judgments that undermine humane feeling (critique of Dante's fabrications of divine wrath is offered as a caution).
